analysis.one_liner: Lets internet users tell websites and apps not to collect their personal data, with FTC enforcement.
analysis.headline: The bill never advanced past its Senate committee and died when the 112th Congress ended in January 2013, without any hearing, vote, or floor action.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have required the Federal Trade Commission to create an easy, one-step way for people to opt out of being tracked online — similar to the 'do not call' list for telemarketers. Websites, apps, and other online services would be barred from collecting personal information about anyone who opted out, except to deliver a service the person actually asked for or where the person saw clear notice and agreed. The FTC and state attorneys general could enforce the rules with fines. The bill was introduced in May 2011, sent to the Senate Commerce Committee, and never received a hearing, a committee vote, or a floor vote before that Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: Internet users who want to stop companies from quietly tracking their browsing, app use, and mobile activity and selling that information for targeted advertising. The bill would also give state attorneys general a new tool to sue violators on behalf of residents.

how_it_helps.text: Requires the FTC to write rules creating a simple mechanism for individuals to indicate they do not want personal information collected by online services, including mobile apps [S2][S3].

Prohibits online service providers from collecting personal information on individuals who have opted out, with narrow exceptions for delivering a requested service (with data anonymized or deleted) or for collection the user affirmatively consents to after clear notice [S2][S3].

Enforces the rules through the FTC and lets state attorneys general sue violators on behalf of residents, with civil penalties up to $16,000 per day of violation (capped at $15 million per violation per person) and inflation adjustments [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Online advertising companies, data brokers, social media platforms, and other internet businesses whose revenue depends on collecting and monetizing behavioral data. Some of the cost could also be passed to users of free, ad-supported services if targeted advertising becomes less effective.
analysis.who_pays_short: Online ad networks and data brokers

drawbacks.text: The bill leaves significant carve-outs: companies could still collect data needed to provide a requested service and could collect nearly anything if the user receives clear notice and affirmatively consents, so tracking could continue through consent prompts [S3].
The bill directs the FTC to weigh the technical feasibility and costs of compliance, giving regulated firms a formal channel to narrow the rules during rulemaking [S3].
State civil penalties are capped at $15 million per violation per person, which limits the maximum financial exposure for the largest firms [S3].

A common objection to do-not-track rules is that much of the free internet is funded by targeted advertising, so a broad opt-out could pressure the ad-supported business model; the bill itself recognizes this by requiring a biennial FTC assessment of the regulations' effect on online commerce [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit — a real, enforceable opt-out from behavioral tracking — is meaningful for anyone who resents being followed across the web, and the exceptions in the bill are reasonably narrow: companies could still run the services users ask for. The main cost falls on the online ad and data industries, with a secondary risk that free ad-supported content would adapt in ways users dislike. The FTC would have had to fill in many details through rulemaking, so the actual strength of the protections would have depended heavily on how the commission wrote the rules.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and sent to the Senate Commerce Committee in May 2011 and sat there — no hearing, no committee vote, no floor vote — until the Congress ended in January 2013 [S5].

narrative.text: Sen. John D. Rockefeller IV introduced the Do-Not-Track Online Act of 2011 in the Senate on May 9, 2011 [S1][S5].
The bill was read twice and referred to the Senate Committee on Commerce, Science, and Transportation the same day [S5].
Two Democratic senators cosponsored the bill [S4].
The action history shows no committee hearing, no markup, no committee report, and no Senate vote after the referral; the last action listed is the May 9, 2011 referral [S5].
The 112th Congress ended on January 3, 2013, and the bill died with it without ever reaching the floor [S1].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Online advertisers, data brokers, and the platforms that profit from behavioral tracking kept operating under the existing no-federal-opt-out regime, since no competing tracking restriction became law in that Congress either.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Online ad networks and data brokers

for.name: Sen. John D. Rockefeller IV
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and made introductory remarks on the Senate floor

for.name: Senate Committee on Commerce, Science, and Transportation
for.what_they_did: Received the bill by referral on the day it was introduced and never reported it out, held no vote on it, and never sent it to the floor

against.name: Online advertising and data-brokerage industry
against.role: Digital ad networks, data brokers, and ad-supported platforms
against.what_they_did: Opposed do-not-track legislation that would restrict behavioral data collection central to targeted-advertising revenue

sides.party_line_note: The record shows only the Democratic sponsor and two Democratic cosponsors and no votes or floor debate, so no partisan pattern can be measured; opposition never had to take a recorded position.

industries.note: Behavioral tracking across websites and apps is the raw material of targeted advertising; a do-not-track mechanism would let users cut off that data stream, directly reducing ad-targeting revenue. Ad industry interests run against the user preference the bill exists to protect.

Firms that collect, aggregate, and sell personal information harvested from online activity would lose access to data from anyone who opted out, and could face FTC and state attorney general enforcement with per-day penalties for violations.

industries.industry: Social media platforms and free online services
industries.note: These services would face compliance costs and reduced access to user data for ad targeting, though the bill preserves collection needed to run the requested service and any collection a user consents to after clear notice.
